body:
Why forests were central to tribal livelihoods

Many tribal communities depended on forests for cultivation, grazing, hunting, fuel, fruit, timber and other produce. Some practised shifting cultivation, also called jhum in parts of India, in which a small area was cleared and cultivated before being left to recover.

Colonial authorities sought timber for railways, construction and commerce. They also wanted fixed settlements and regular revenue collections. These objectives frequently conflicted with customary forest use and tribal systems of landholding.

Forest legislation and its effects

The Indian Forest Act of 1865 strengthened colonial control over forests. The 1878 legislation classified forests into reserved, protected and village forests. The forest law was further revised in 1927.

Restrictions varied according to the legal category and local rules. In reserved forests, access to wood, grazing, cultivation and other forest produce could be severely limited. These restrictions disrupted daily livelihoods and sometimes forced forest communities to move or work for the Forest Department.

Colonial expansion also increased the influence of moneylenders, traders, contractors and landlords. Among the Mundas, the word diku was used for outsiders associated with domination and exploitation. Such outsiders could include landlords, traders and moneylenders; the term did not refer to one particular official post.

Important tribal uprisings

Kol Uprising, 1831–1832

The Kol Uprising occurred in the Chotanagpur region. Tribal discontent was connected with the growing power of outsiders, changes in landholding and exploitation. It is an important early example of armed tribal resistance to colonial-era changes.

Santhal Hul, 1855–1856

The Santhal Hul was a major rebellion in the region of the Rajmahal Hills and Santhal settlements. Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu were prominent leaders. Santhals opposed exploitation by moneylenders, landlords and colonial authorities. The movement began in 1855.

The word Hul is associated with rebellion or uprising. The Santhal movement should not be confused with Birsa Munda's later movement in Chotanagpur.

Birsa Munda and the Ulgulan, 1899–1900

Birsa Munda organised an important movement among the Mundas of Chotanagpur. He challenged the domination of outsiders and sought restoration of customary community rights over land. His movement also encouraged social reform within tribal society.

The uprising of 1899–1900 is commonly called the Ulgulan, or Great Tumult. Birsa was arrested and died in jail in 1900.

Bastar Rebellion, 1910

In Bastar, present-day Chhattisgarh, the proposed reservation of large forest areas threatened shifting cultivation, hunting and the collection of forest produce. Demands for unpaid labour and earlier economic distress increased resentment.

The rebellion broke out in 1910. The Dhurwa community played an important part, and Gunda Dhur of Nethanar is remembered as an important figure. The movement involved several communities and did not have a single universally acknowledged leader.

Tana Bhagat Movement, from 1914

The Tana Bhagat Movement began among the Oraons of Chotanagpur under Jatra Oraon in 1914. It combined religious and social reform with resistance to oppressive rent and forced labour demands. Sections of the movement later associated themselves with Gandhian non-cooperation.

Rampa or Gudem Hills Rebellion, 1922–1924

In the Gudem Hills of the Andhra region, forest restrictions and demands for begar, including road-building labour, caused widespread resentment.

Alluri Sitarama Raju led an armed resistance movement during 1922–1924. Although he admired Gandhi and encouraged some Gandhian practices, he believed that armed struggle was necessary. The rebels attacked police stations and fought colonial forces. Raju was captured and executed in 1924.

Not every tribal movement followed the same method. The Rampa rebellion used armed resistance, while the Tana Bhagat movement became associated with non-violent practices. Their shared feature was opposition to conditions that threatened tribal livelihoods, dignity or customary rights.

Prelims focus

  • 1878 forest classification: reserved, protected and village forests.
  • Santhal Hul, 1855–1856: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu.
  • Munda Ulgulan, 1899–1900: Birsa Munda, Chotanagpur.
  • Bastar Rebellion, 1910: Gunda Dhur.
  • Tana Bhagat Movement, from 1914: Jatra Oraon.
  • Rampa Rebellion, 1922–1924: Alluri Sitarama Raju.
  • Trap: Birsa Munda and Alluri Sitarama Raju led different movements in different regions.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age, printed pp. 39–50; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–I, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, chapter Forest Society and Colonialism, printed pp. 83–92; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 59–60; Ministry of Culture, Dictionary of Martyrs: India's Freedom Struggle (1857–1947), entry on Birsa Munda, consulted 22 November 2026; J. Dasgupta, Reading Adivasi Histories: Tana Bhagats in Colonial Times, section on the movement's beginnings, consulted 22 November 2026.]

body:
The importance of Gujarat's tribal regions

Tribal resistance in western India extended across areas that today belong to Gujarat, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. Present-day state boundaries should not obscure the regional connections among Bhil communities and other forest-dependent groups.

The movements differed in their immediate aims. Some challenged forced labour and oppressive revenue demands. Others emphasised social reform, temperance and independence from exploitative creditors. Several later developed connections with the wider nationalist movement.

Govind Guru and the Mangarh gathering, 1913

Govind Guru, also known as Govindgiri, became an important organiser among Bhil communities. His activities combined social reform with opposition to forms of exploitation, including forced labour.

On 17 November 1913, colonial forces fired on a large Bhil gathering at Mangarh Hill in the Banswara region of present-day Rajasthan. The incident is remembered as the Mangarh massacre. Official commemorations describe very large casualties, although historical estimates of the number killed are not uniform.

Mangarh has an important Gujarat connection because its participants and commemorative significance extend across the Rajasthan–Gujarat tribal region. However, Mangarh Hill itself is in Rajasthan, not Gujarat.

Motilal Tejawat and the Eki Movement

The Eki Movement developed during 1921–1922 in the Mewar region and neighbouring tribal areas. Motilal Tejawat mobilised Bhil and other rural communities against oppressive land revenue, forced labour and feudal demands.

The movement spread into parts of northern Gujarat, including areas associated with Danta, Khedbrahma and the former Idar State. The word eki conveyed the idea of unity among participants.

Pal-Dadhvav massacre, 7 March 1922

As part of the Eki mobilisation, villagers assembled near Pal-Chitariya and Dadhvav, in the area of present-day Sabarkantha district, Gujarat. The gathering took place on 7 March 1922.

Armed forces fired upon the gathering, causing many deaths. The incident is remembered as the Pal-Dadhvav massacre. Reported casualty totals differ between accounts, so the event should be identified principally by its established date, place and connection with Motilal Tejawat's movement.

Mangarh, 1913 and Pal-Dadhvav, 1922 were different incidents. Mangarh is associated with Govind Guru and is located in present-day Rajasthan. Pal-Dadhvav is associated with Motilal Tejawat's Eki Movement and is located in present-day Gujarat.

The Devi Movement in South Gujarat, 1922–1923

The Devi Movement spread among tribal communities in South Gujarat during 1922–1923. It encouraged abstinence from liquor and toddy and promoted changes in community practices. Its followers also challenged dependence on exploitative liquor dealers, creditors and landlords.

Its immediate programme was not identical to an armed uprising against the British government. It combined social reform, economic resistance and community mobilisation. Gandhian workers later developed connections with sections of the movement, linking local reform to broader nationalist activity.

This example shows that tribal political participation was not limited to armed rebellions. Social discipline, boycotts and campaigns against economic dependence could also become means of collective action.

Connecting tribal and peasant struggles in Gujarat

Gujarat's nationalist history includes both the revenue-based peasant satyagrahas of Kheda and Bardoli and the tribal mobilisation of the borderlands and South Gujarat. Their histories overlapped geographically and politically, but they should not be treated as identical.

For example, the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 centred on an enhanced land revenue assessment. The Devi Movement of 1922–1923 centred on tribal reform and resistance to exploitative social and economic relations. Understanding the difference is more useful than memorising the word Gujarat alone.

Prelims focus

  • Mangarh massacre: 17 November 1913; Govind Guru; present-day Rajasthan.
  • Eki Movement: associated with Motilal Tejawat and the Rajasthan–Gujarat tribal belt.
  • Pal-Dadhvav massacre: 7 March 1922; present-day Sabarkantha, Gujarat.
  • Devi Movement: South Gujarat, 1922–1923; temperance and resistance to exploitation.
  • Trap: Do not interchange the leaders or locations of Mangarh and Pal-Dadhvav.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Mangarh Dham ki Gaurav Gatha, press release of November 2022, background on the 17 November 1913 gathering, consulted 22 November 2026; The Indian Express, Explained: What Was the Pal-Dadhvav Massacre?, 8 March 2022, sections The Incident and the Eki Movement, consulted 22 November 2026; IGNOU, Anti-Colonial Tribal Movements in India, Unit 15, section 15.5.6, Devi Movement in Gujarat (1922–23), consulted 22 November 2026; Ministry of Tribal Affairs research repository, Socio-Religious Movements among Tribals of South Gujarat, chapter Devi Movement, consulted 22 November 2026.]

body:
Industrial workers and the colonial economy

The growth of textile mills, railways, mines, ports and plantations created new groups of wage earners. Many workers faced long hours, low wages, unsafe conditions and harsh disciplinary practices.

Industrial labour refers here to workers employed in factories, mines and related establishments for wages. Plantation labour refers to workers employed on estates growing crops such as tea. Their circumstances differed: industrial workers often organised around wages and working hours, while plantation workers could also face severe restrictions on movement.

A trade union is an organisation through which workers collectively represent their interests, raise demands and negotiate or protest over conditions of employment.

Early worker organisation

Narayan Meghaji Lokhande was associated with the Bombay Millhands Association during the late nineteenth century. It was an important early attempt to represent textile workers' concerns.

The Madras Labour Union was established on 27 April 1918 among workers associated with the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills. B. P. Wadia became its first president, and T. V. Kalyanasundara Mudaliar was among the important organisers. The union pressed for better treatment, wages and working conditions.

Ahmedabad Mill Strike and the Textile Labour Association

In 1918, textile mill workers in Ahmedabad, Gujarat became involved in a major wage dispute. Gandhi supported the workers' struggle through satyagraha, while Anasuya Sarabhai played an important organising role.

Gandhi encouraged disciplined non-violent action and negotiation. The Ahmedabad episode became an important example of his approach to relations between labour and employers.

In 1920, the Textile Labour Association, also known as the Majoor Mahajan Sangh, developed in Ahmedabad. Its formation was closely associated with Anasuya Sarabhai, Mahatma Gandhi and Shankerlal Banker. Gandhi formally inaugurated a constituent union of throttle workers on 25 February 1920.

The Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918 was an industrial dispute. The Textile Labour Association of 1920 was an organised union structure that developed afterward. Their dates should not be interchanged.

All India Trade Union Congress, 1920

The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was established in Bombay on 31 October 1920. It brought workers' organisations onto a wider national platform. Lala Lajpat Rai became its first president. Other early figures included N. M. Joshi, Joseph Baptista and Diwan Chaman Lall.

The Trade Unions Act, 1926 provided a legal framework for the registration of trade unions. It was an important institutional development for organised labour.

Workers in the national movements

Workers joined nationalist campaigns, but their participation varied by region, industry and political circumstances. Some used nationalist boycotts alongside demands for improved wages and working conditions.

During the Civil Disobedience Movement, industrial workers did not participate in uniformly large numbers. The Nagpur region was an important exception. Railway workers struck in 1930, and dockworkers took strike action in 1932. After Gandhi's arrest in 1930, workers in Sholapur took part in militant protests against symbols of colonial authority.

Congress leaders were often cautious about including strong labour demands in the national programme because Indian industrialists were also important supporters of the anti-colonial movement.

Assam tea plantation workers

Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, plantation workers in Assam were subject to restrictions on leaving the tea gardens without permission. During the Non-Cooperation Movement, thousands attempted to leave plantations and return to their home villages. Many were stopped, stranded and subjected to repression.

For these workers, swaraj included a concrete demand: freedom of movement and release from restrictive plantation conditions. This differed from the usual industrial demand for higher wages or shorter hours.

Prelims focus

  • Madras Labour Union: 27 April 1918; B. P. Wadia.
  • Ahmedabad Mill Strike: 1918; Gandhi and Anasuya Sarabhai.
  • Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad: 1920; also called Majoor Mahajan Sangh.
  • AITUC: established on 31 October 1920 in Bombay; first president Lala Lajpat Rai.
  • Trade Unions Act: 1926.
  • Assam plantation workers faced restrictions associated with the Inland Emigration Act of 1859.
  • Trap: AITUC was a national federation; the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association was a city-based labour organisation.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 115–117; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 60 and 66; Archives of Indian Labour, community history All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), consulted 22 November 2026; Archives of Indian Labour, The Madras Labour Union (of the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills), institutional record and historical account, consulted 22 November 2026; Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad, Six Decades of Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad (1917–1977), Major Events: Period of Spade Work, printed p. 5, 1977; V. V. Giri National Labour Institute, Evolution of Trade Unions in India, section Madras Labour Union, consulted 22 November 2026.]
